# Pipelines and Hazards

## Concepts

A pipeline separates work into stages so that multiple transactions can be in flight. Latency counts the cycles between acceptance and completion; throughput counts completed transactions per unit time. Increasing stage count can shorten combinational paths while increasing latency and control complexity.

An elastic pipeline adds valid state and backpressure to each stage. A stalled consumer must not cause a producer to overwrite pending data. Instruction pipelines require additional rules: operands may depend on unfinished instructions, branches can invalidate younger work, and exceptions must preserve architectural ordering.

## Implementation

Use the one-entry ready/valid buffer in the SystemVerilog chapter as a transport building block. Its occupancy transition is:

```text
input_fire  = in_valid  && in_ready
output_fire = out_valid && out_ready
next_occupancy = occupancy + input_fire - output_fire
```

Outside reset, occupancy remains either zero or one. Replacement is legal when both transfers occur together. Chaining these buffers adds forward registers but also creates a combinational ready chain. A skid buffer or a different buffering protocol is needed when the backward path must also be registered.

For CORE-V Wally analysis, separately identify the logic that stalls stages, forwards operands, and flushes instructions. A generic transport buffer alone does not implement dependency checking or correct exception handling.

## Hands-on Experiments

Connect two elastic stages and send numbered payloads while varying downstream readiness. Check ordering and conservation: accepted inputs minus accepted outputs must equal the number of occupied stages. Measure empty-pipeline latency and sustained throughput.

Then add a flush requirement to the specification before modifying RTL. Define whether pending transactions are discarded and whether simultaneous input is accepted. Compare this transport-level flush with the instruction-level requirements of a processor.
